passages.t: The siege, and a king caught at Jericho
passages.happening:
In the ninth year of Zedekiah, on the tenth day of the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar comes against Jerusalem with his whole army and builds a siege wall around it (verse 1). The siege lasts until Zedekiah's eleventh year. ‘By the ninth day of the fourth month, the famine in the city was so severe that the people of the land had no food’ (verse 3).

The city is breached, and the soldiers flee by night through the gate between the two walls, toward the Arabah (verse 4). The Chaldean army overtakes the king in the plains of Jericho, and his army scatters (verse 5). They bring him to the king of Babylon at Riblah, where sentence is passed on him (verse 6). His sons are killed in front of him, and he is blinded, bound in bronze shackles and taken to Babylon (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
This is the end of the story that began in 1 Kings with Solomon's temple and David's throne. Everything the prophets warned of happens. The chapter is told with restraint: almost no speeches, no prophecies and no comment. The narrator has already explained the fall more than once, and now he lets the events speak. Dates are given to the day, as in a record of mourning.

The siege began in the winter of 588 or 587 BC, and the city was breached about eighteen months later, in the summer of 587 or 586 BC. Scholars differ over the exact years because of different ways of counting a king's years. The site's guide to the kings follows Thiele's 586, and notes that many historians prefer 587. Jeremiah names Lachish and Azekah as the last fortified cities holding out, and inked potsherds found at Lachish, the Lachish letters, are military messages from those last months. Riblah in Syria was Nebuchadnezzar's field headquarters.

Zedekiah had sworn loyalty to Nebuchadnezzar, and Ezekiel treats his rebellion as an oath broken in the LORD's name. What was done to him and his sons was a known punishment for a rebel vassal in that world, meant to end his line. The text tells it in one verse, and these notes do not dwell on it.
passages.later: Jeremiah wrote of the last days, when the army of Babylon fought ‘against Lachish and Azekah. For these were the only fortified cities remaining in Judah’ (Jeremiah 34:7).
passages.asks: The king fled by night and was caught in the plains of Jericho, where Israel had first entered the land. Ask what it means that the story ends near where it began. And ask what promises you have broken under pressure, and what they cost those you love.

passages.t: The house of the LORD burned
passages.happening:
On the seventh day of the fifth month, in Nebuchadnezzar's nineteenth year, Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, enters Jerusalem (verse 8). ‘He burned down the house of the LORD, the royal palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem’ (verse 9). The army breaks down the walls (verse 10). Nebuzaradan carries the rest of the people into exile and leaves some of the poorest to tend the vineyards and fields (verses 11-12).

The Chaldeans break up the bronze pillars, the stands and the bronze Sea and carry the bronze to Babylon, with the pots, shovels, dishes and every article of the temple's service (verses 13-15). The bronze from Solomon's pillars, Sea and stands is beyond weighing (verse 16).

Nebuzaradan takes the chief priest Seraiah, the second priest Zephaniah, the doorkeepers, officials and sixty men of the city to the king of Babylon at Riblah, and they are put to death there (verses 18-21). ‘So Judah was taken into exile, away from its own land’ (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Burning a conquered city's temple was also a political statement. In the thinking of the time, a people's god had been defeated along with them. The list of bronze recalls the account of Solomon's temple in 1 Kings 7 item by item, as if the building were being unmade in reverse.

Excavations in Jerusalem have found signs of the city's burning: collapsed houses, layers of ash and arrowheads from this time. The days of the siege and the fall became fixed in Jewish memory as days of fasting, and Zechariah later names fasts in the fourth, fifth, seventh and tenth months.

Verse 21 sounds like the book's final verdict. The word for exile, galah, is the one used of the northern tribes in 17:6. The land had been the sign of God's covenant gift, and losing it was the covenant's heaviest curse.
passages.later: Lamentations grieves the city: “How lonely lies the city, once so full of people!” (Lamentations 1:1). A psalm asks, ‘Where, O Lord, is Your loving devotion of old, which You faithfully swore to David?’ (Psalm 89:49). And from the ruins Lamentations says, ‘Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail’ (Lamentations 3:22).
passages.hard:
If God chose Jerusalem and promised David an everlasting throne, how could he let the city and the temple burn? And what does this chapter say about suffering, then and now?

This was the question that faced the exiles, and much of the Old Testament wrestles with it. Lamentations grieves the city's fall without pretending to understand everything, and Psalm 89 cries out that God seems to have renounced his covenant with David. Both are in the Bible. Kings gives its own answer: the promise to David had always carried conditions for each king, and the city fell because king and people broke the covenant again and again, despite generations of warning. The destruction does not show that God was unfaithful. It shows that he meant what he said.

Kings also hints that the promise itself was not withdrawn. The line of David survives in Jehoiachin, and the book ends with him alive and honored. The prophets of the exile, Jeremiah and Ezekiel among them, promised a return, a renewed covenant and a future king of David's line.

This is Judah's own Scripture, judging Judah's own kings and grieving Judah's own losses. It was written for people who had lost everything, to help them understand their history and turn back to God. It is not a key for reading anyone else's suffering. It gives no one a warrant to say that any people's suffering, then or now, is a punishment they deserved: not a city under siege, not a people driven from its home, not a family that has lost everything. And it is never a reason to blame the Jewish people, then or now. The voice of the book is grief, and its last word is mercy.

A word for anyone who has lived through a flood, a storm or another disaster. Your loss was not a judgment on you. When Jesus was asked about people killed when a tower fell, he refused that reading of a disaster: “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you are carrying this, you need people more than explanations. Please talk to someone you trust, and the Find Help page has people you can call.
passages.asks: The temple, the city and the throne all fell, and God's mercies did not. Ask what this chapter teaches about the difference between God's presence and the religious structures built around it. And ask how you would grieve, and whom you would grieve with, if what you had built were lost.

passages.happening:
Nebuchadnezzar appoints Gedaliah son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, over the people left in the land (verse 22). The army commanders and their men come to him at Mizpah, and he swears to them, “Do not be afraid of the servants of the Chaldeans. Live in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will be well with you” (verse 24).

In the seventh month Ishmael son of Nethaniah, a member of the royal family, comes with ten men and kills Gedaliah and the Judeans and Chaldeans with him at Mizpah (verse 25). Then all the people, small and great, with the army commanders, flee to Egypt for fear of the Chaldeans (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
Gedaliah was the grandson of Shaphan, whose family had supported Jeremiah. He governed from Mizpah, a few miles north of Jerusalem. Jeremiah tells his story more fully, including the flight to Egypt that took Jeremiah with it. His murder was later remembered with a fast in the seventh month.

Each section of the chapter strips away something more: the city, the temple, the leaders, and now the remnant's fragile hope of living in the land. Gedaliah's counsel was the same as Jeremiah's: live in the land, serve the king of Babylon, and it will go well. Violence cut it short.
passages.later: Jeremiah gives Gedaliah's oath in nearly the same words: ‘Live in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will go well with you’ (Jeremiah 40:9).
passages.asks: Gedaliah told the survivors to live and rebuild, and violence ended that hope. Ask how people rebuild after a catastrophe, and what makes that work so fragile. And ask how you might protect those who are trying to rebuild near you.

passages.happening: On the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month of the thirty-seventh year of Jehoiachin's exile, in the year Evil-merodach becomes king of Babylon, he releases King Jehoiachin of Judah from prison (verse 27). ‘And he spoke kindly to Jehoiachin and set his throne above the thrones of the other kings who were with him in Babylon’ (verse 28). ‘So Jehoiachin changed out of his prison clothes, and he dined regularly at the king’s table for the rest of his life’ (verse 29). ‘And the king provided Jehoiachin a daily portion for the rest of his life’ (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
Evil-merodach, Amel-Marduk in Babylonian sources, was Nebuchadnezzar's son and reigned from 562 to 560 BC. He released Jehoiachin early in his reign, about 561 BC. The picture of a captive king fed at the Babylonian court fits documents found in Babylon: tablets from Nebuchadnezzar's reign, some thirty years earlier, list rations of oil issued to Jehoiachin, king of Judah, and his sons.

Eating at the king's table was a mark of high favor and protection, and a daily allowance for life meant security for the rest of one's days. The word for the throne he is given, kisse, is the word for the throne of David, the great promise of Kings. It is not David's throne in Jerusalem, but the word keeps the promise in mind. The word for his daily portion, aruchah, is a modest word to end a book on: survival, provision and a future not yet known.

The book does not end in ashes. The words for the rest of his life close it twice, open-ended, with a son of David still alive and honored. The writer does not explain why he ends here. Readers have long seen in it a small light.
passages.later: The scene recalls David's kindness to Saul's grandson: ‘So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, because he always ate at the king’s table’ (2 Samuel 9:13). Matthew counts ‘fourteen from David to the exile to Babylon, and fourteen from the exile to the Christ’ (Matthew 1:17).
passages.asks: Kings ends with a small kindness to a prisoner rather than a restored kingdom. Ask where you have seen God's faithfulness in small, quiet signs during a season of loss. And ask what it would mean for you to change out of your prison clothes.
